lead: Some patients need a radioactivity measurement: a thyroid uptake study, a hormone assay, a sample in a hot lab. Ionising radiation is invisible, so we detect what it does — it knocks electrons off atoms. In a gas it makes ion pairs, and the Geiger–Müller tube turns each event into one large pulse. In a crystal it makes a flash of light, and a photomultiplier turns that flash into a pulse whose height follows the radiation energy.
prereq: You need the photodetector and photomultiplier idea from 3.1.

sections.h3: Radiation units and the Geiger–Müller tube

blocks.text: Activity is decays per second, in becquerel (Bq): 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. The older curie (Ci) is 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq. Absorbed dose is energy deposited per kilogram of the material absorbing it, in gray (Gy): 1 Gy = 1 J/kg. Equivalent dose is absorbed dose multiplied by a radiation weighting factor for the harm each radiation type does, in sievert (Sv), which is also 1 J/kg; the factor is 1 for gamma rays and beta particles and 20 for alpha particles, so for gamma rays 1 Gy gives 1 Sv.

The GM tube is a metal cylinder with a thin window, filled with argon at low pressure plus a little halogen or alcohol vapour, the quench gas. A fine axial wire is the anode at a few hundred volts positive; the wall is the cathode.

A gamma ray or beta particle ionises argon. Electrons drift to the wire, gain energy in the steep field near it and ionise more argon, so an avalanche builds and the tube discharges briefly. One event gives one pulse of about 1 V, whatever energy the radiation carried.

The quench gas absorbs the discharge photons and stops the avalanche, so the tube recovers. Count rate against voltage is flat over the Geiger plateau, usually 350–500 V, and the tube runs mid-plateau. Every pulse is the same size, so the tube counts radiation but cannot name the isotope. After each pulse the tube is blind for a dead time τ of 100–200 µs, so some events are lost at high count rates. The true rate is found from the observed rate:

blocks.where: n is the true count rate and m the observed count rate, in counts per second; τ is the dead time in s; mτ is the fraction of time the tube is dead.

sections.h3: Scintillation counter and the gamma spectrum

blocks.text: A thallium-activated sodium iodide crystal, NaI(Tl), absorbs a gamma ray and emits a light flash whose brightness follows the energy deposited. A photomultiplier tube (PMT) has a photocathode that turns the flash into electrons and a dynode chain that multiplies them about a million times, giving an electrical pulse.

Pulse height follows gamma energy. A multichannel analyser sorts pulses by height into channels and plots counts against energy: the gamma spectrum. The photopeak position identifies the isotope, which the GM tube cannot do.

Tritium and carbon-14 beta particles are too weak to reach a crystal, so the sample is dissolved in a liquid scintillation cocktail and flashes are counted from inside. Clinical uses include radioimmunoassay with iodine-125 and thyroid uptake studies.

Safety is lead shielding, short time near the source and distance: the dose rate from a small source falls as 1/(distance)², so doubling the distance cuts it to a quarter. Staff wear film or thermoluminescent badges to record dose.

spec.aria: Cylindrical tube with a thin window, an axial anode wire fed from a 425 volt supply through a resistor, a capacitor to an amplifier and scaler, and below a curve of count rate against voltage rising at 300 volts, flat from 350 to 500 volts and rising again above.

examples.question: A Geiger–Müller counter gives 12 000 counts in 5.0 min with a source present and 200 counts in 5.0 min with the source removed. The counting efficiency is 20 %. Find the net count rate and the activity of the source.
steps: Both counts are taken over the same time: t = 5.0 min = 300 s.
Gross count rate = 12 000 / 300 s = 40.0 counts per second; background rate = 200 / 300 s = 0.67 counts per second.
Net counts = 12 000 − 200 = 11 800, so net count rate = 11 800 / 300 s = 39.33 counts per second.
Activity A = net count rate / efficiency = 39.33 / 0.20 = 196.67 Bq.
examples.answer: The net count rate is about 39.3 counts per second and the source activity is about 197 Bq.

gross=12000
bg=200
t=5.0*60
gross_rate=gross/t
bg_rate=bg/t
net_rate=(gross-bg)/t

A=net_rate/eff
print(round(gross_rate,2))
print(round(bg_rate,2))

examples.question: A GM counter with a dead time of 200 µs records 1000 counts per second from a sample. Find the true count rate and the fraction of events lost.
steps: mτ = 1000 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.20, so the tube is dead for 20 % of each second.
Lost events = 1250 − 1000 = 250 per second, which is 250 / 1250 = 20 % of the true rate.
examples.answer: The true rate is 1250 counts per second; 20 % of the events are lost in the dead time.

traps: Forgetting to subtract the background count, or reporting raw counts instead of counts per second.

Claiming the GM pulse height tells you the radiation energy — it does not; energy information comes from detectors whose pulse height follows deposited energy, such as the scintillation counter, proportional counter or a semiconductor detector.
Mixing the units: curie is activity (1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq), gray is absorbed dose, sievert is equivalent dose.
Treating dead time as microseconds of no consequence: at 5000 counts per second with 200 µs dead time the tube is effectively saturated.
Setting the GM voltage anywhere on the plateau without checking it is a flat region — below it counts are lost, above it the tube discharges continuously.

quiz.q: Define becquerel, gray and sievert, and give the curie in becquerel.
quiz.a: 1 Bq = 1 decay per second; 1 Gy = 1 J/kg of energy absorbed in any material; 1 Sv = 1 J/kg of equivalent dose, that is absorbed dose in Gy multiplied by the radiation weighting factor (1 for gamma rays, so 1 Gy gives 1 Sv); 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq.

quiz.q: Why is every Geiger–Müller pulse the same height?
quiz.a: The avalanche spreads along the whole anode, so the pulse size is set by the tube and its circuit, not by how much energy the particle deposited. Counting is possible; energy measurement is not.

quiz.q: A GM counter gives 3600 counts in 3.0 min with a source and 180 counts in 3.0 min without it. Find the net count rate.
quiz.a: t = 180 s. Gross rate = 3600/180 = 20 s⁻¹; background = 180/180 = 1.0 s⁻¹; net rate = (3600 − 180)/180 = 19 counts per second.

quiz.q: Why is liquid scintillation used for tritium instead of a NaI(Tl) crystal?
quiz.a: Tritium beta particles are very weak and cannot cross the crystal window or the air gap. Dissolving the sample in the cocktail puts the emitter in direct contact with the scintillator, so every decay can be counted.

quiz.q: Why is the GM tube operated in the middle of the plateau and not at its lower edge?
quiz.a: Mid-plateau a small drift in the high-voltage supply barely changes the count rate. At the lower edge the avalanches are incomplete, so counts depend strongly on voltage; above the plateau the tube discharges continuously and counts falsely.

quiz.q: A source gives about 5000 counts per second and the tube dead time is 200 µs. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: Dead-time fraction = observed rate × dead time = 5000 s⁻¹ × 200 × 10⁻⁶ s = 1.0. The tube can never deliver more than 1/τ = 5000 counts per second, so at this rate it is saturated: it is dead between pulses and the true rate is much higher than 5000 per second. Dilute the sample or apply a dead-time correction.

beyond: Not for the exam. Hospital hot labs elute technetium-99m from a generator each morning and check it on a dose calibrator, an ionisation chamber rather than a counter. Modern gamma counters use NaI(Tl) or solid-state cadmium zinc telluride detectors with digital multichannel analysers, and software corrects dead time and background and marks the photopeak automatically. Search for 'gamma spectrum photopeak', 'dead time correction' and 'liquid scintillation counting' to go further.
